247 PM EDT Sat Aug 1 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 241 PM EDT Saturday...

Have increased the rainfall totals across the St. Lawrence Valley 
and portions of the Adirondacks to range between 1 to 1.5 
inches, with locally higher amounts possible within any 
convective activity. An isolated flash flood threat across 
northern New York remains for late Sunday into early Monday with
slow-moving showers and thunderstorms possible.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 241 PM EDT Saturday...

1. Showers and embedded thunderstorms will increase across the 
region Sunday into Monday. Locally heavy rainfall possible, 
especially in the St. Lawrence Valley.

2. A chance of showers and thunderstorms persists over the second 
half of next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 241 PM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A slow moving upper level trough with associated closed 
surface low is currently centered across the Ohio Valley and will 
track to the east northeast today into tomorrow. A baroclinic zone 
is also set up across the Great Lakes and eastern Ontario bringing 
some isolated shower chances today across the St. Lawrence Valley. 
As this system tracks east, cloud cover will increase areawide into 
tonight with south to southwest channeled flow just above the 
surface, which should help limit, or prevent altogether, the 
coverage of any potential fog tonight. 

Into tomorrow, the system will approach the St. Lawrence Valley and 
the North Country with shower chances increasing by midday Sunday. 
Thermodynamic profiles denote some skinny SBCAPE between 500-
1000J/kg which will allow for at least some isolated convection and 
thunderstorm activity. This activity will likely be confined to near 
the St. Lawrence River and along US-11 in St. Lawrence County. 
Modest to weak mid level flow between 20-30 knots with Pwats 
approaching 1.8-2", and deep warm layer cloud depths, locally heavy 
rain within any convection will be possible. WPC has kept the St. 
Lawrence Valley in a Slight (Risk level 2 out of 4) for a at least a 
15% chance of exceeding flash flood guidance. The axis of these 
showers remains somewhat variable from run to run across the Hi Res 
CAMs. The NAM3 keeps much of the convective activity during the day 
tomorrow over the border in Ontario, whereas the HRRR rides the axis 
of instability over western St. Lawrence County. Where this 
deformation boundary sets up will have a large impact on the total 
rainfall from this system. Right now have kept the convective 
activity on the US side of the border with a more stable run to run 
consistent HRRR solution. Should an area see repeated rounds of 
showers, especially with antecedent rainfall, flash flooding cannot 
be ruled out. However, the St. Lawrence Valley at the present time 
is not expected to see significant enough rainfall to produce 
flooding over the prevailing flatter terrain. 

Towards Sunday evening and Sunday night, the deformation boundary 
will shift east into the Champlain Valley and Vermont by Monday 
morning. There is good agreement that overnight Sunday should have 
the better rainfall coverage and contain the bulk of the rainfall. A 
few areas of brief 0.25-0.5 inch/hour rates will be possible across 
northern New York within the boundary as it shifts east towards 
Vermont. Showers will slowly taper off by Monday afternoon across 
eastern Vermont with fog development likely in the valleys of the 
region with brief high pressure nudging in. Currently have increased 
rainfall totals across the St. Lawrence Valley, with new guidance. 
Total rainfall for most of the region will be around 0.5 inches. 
Locally higher amounts between an inch to an inch an a half will be 
possible from the foothills of the Adirondacks into the St. Lawrence 
Valley, especially under any convective activity. Tuesday will be 
drier and calmer with temperatures in the upper 70s to low 80s and 
clearing skies.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A slow moving to stationary front will be draped across our 
region for the second half of next week bringing repeated rounds of 
showers and thunderstorms.  While the showers will linger through 
multiple days, the thermodynamic profiles don't look to support severe 
potential as we are seeing 250-500 J/kg of CAPE each afternoon with 
weak shear. These values will support air mass/popcorn thunderstorms 
with a few rumbles of thunder and short lived localized heavy rain. 
Consistent with a stationary front, temperatures will be remarkably 
consistent over the period. Daytime highs in the warmest valleys will 
be in the mid-80s daily with overnight lows falling into the mid-60s. 
The stationary front will finally move off at the end of next week as a 
low pressure will move in from the southeastern US bring more 
organization to the thunderstorms and the possibility of stronger 
convection.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Through 18Z Sunday...VFR conditions will persist through the day
today. A scattered to broken deck of fair weather Cu will continue
to develop into the afternoon hours with a cirrus deck above. Last
night saw the development of fog in many of our favored locations,
and the low level moisture remains available. However, the low
pressure to our west will bring increased winds and clouds overnight
inhibiting pure radiational effects. For now, I'm including some
shallow fog development at MPV and SLK near sunrise but don't
anticipate widespread formation like we had last night.

Outlook...

Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Likely SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Monday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Definite SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Monday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Tuesday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Tuesday Night: VFR. Slight chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Wednesday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Chance TSRA.
Wednesday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Thursday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.

&&
